fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. The text says "A wise servant will rule over a disgraceful son…" Think about that. A servant over a son. I'd have to read that twice.
No foreign king shows up in this saying. No crowns, no armies, no royal visits. The one who rules over the disgraceful son is a wise servant, who also shares the inheritance as one of the brothers.
A nice guess, but the verse never mentions a field. It says the servant will "…share his inheritance as one of the brothers." So the answer is a share of the inheritance, not a field of his own.
You've got it. "Eloquent words are unfit for a fool; how much worse are lying lips to a ruler!" Lying lips on a ruler are the worse thing. That's the comparison the saying makes.

Yes, baker. "A rebuke cuts into a man of discernment deeper than a hundred lashes cut into a fool." A rebuke on one side and a hundred lashes on the other. And it's the rebuke that cuts deeper into the man of discernment.
Not quite, baker. The verse says "…abandon the dispute before it breaks out." The moment it names is before it breaks out. Once it's heated is a different moment than the one the verse points to.
Right, baker. "Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous—both are detestable to the LORD." He names both verdicts. The word is both, and avoiding just one isn't what the verse says.

Land is a fair guess, but the verse has something else in mind. The fool has money in his hand "…with no intention of buying wisdom?" Money in his hand, and wisdom nowhere on his shopping list. I've had a few shopping trips like that myself.

Wise from a broken spirit would be a nice twist, but this verse doesn't go there. It says "A joyful heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries up the bones." Dried-up bones are what the verse names. I'll take the medicine, baker.
Yes, baker. The wicked man takes the bribe "…to subvert the course of justice." That's what the covert bribe is for. The aim is to turn justice off its course.
Paying off debts? I wish my bills were that simple. The verse says "A wicked man takes a covert bribe to subvert the course of justice." Justice is what he's messing with, not his debts.

That's right, baker. "…the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth." Right beside it, "Wisdom is the focus of the discerning…" Two pictures side by side: eyes locked on one thing, and eyes all over the map.

Yes, baker. "It is surely not good to punish the innocent or to flog a noble for his honesty." Punishing someone who did nothing wrong is not good. The verse says it plainly. The same saying says it about flogging a noble for his honesty too.

Sharp words do sound clever, I'll give you that. But the verse says "A man of knowledge restrains his words…" He holds them back instead of sharpening them. I've sharpened a few of mine and cut myself every time.

Gifts would be a fun way to get called wise, but they aren't in this saying. The verse says "Even a fool is considered wise if he keeps silent, and discerning when he holds his tongue." Zip the lips and the title shows up for free. Keeping silent is the answer.
